traveler: Ahmad al-Majriti (the name over the Rutbat al-Hakim and the Ghayat al-Hakim; in the sources a patronymic, ibn Ahmad, son of Ahmad)
title: The Son of Ahmad: A Patronymic Comes Loose and Travels Nine Centuries Under Its Own Name
years: c. 906-1007 (the men behind the name); 1360-2026 (the name in transit)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Nisba and the Father's Name

stops.name: Majrit, the fortress above the Manzanares
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Umayyad foundation of Majrit is placed in the reign of Muhammad I and no source consulted fixes a year
stops.campa: On a bluff over the Manzanares the Umayyads keep a fortress and a garrison town, Majrit, set to watch the road that runs from the northern kingdoms down toward Toledo. It is a frontier posting and never a capital. Men who leave it for the caliphal south carry the town behind their own names as a nisba, al-Majriti, the one from Majrit, and the word outlasts the fort, the caliphate, and every man who wears it. Every candidate in the tangle is fastened to this hill by one adjective and by nothing else at all.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad fortress of Majrit, root of the nisba al-Majriti

stops.name: Madrid, the Arab wall at the Cuesta de la Vega
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the surviving wall is dated broadly to the ninth and tenth centuries and the placement here carries no source year
stops.campa: Below the Cuesta de la Vega a run of flint and limestone still stands, the oldest built thing in the city that grew out of the fort. It is what remains of the town the nisba points at. No register of births survives from Majrit, no roll of its scholars, no list of the households that sent sons to Cordoba. For most men out of this place the name is the only fact of origin that reaches a biographer, and a name is exactly the kind of evidence that copies wrong.
suggested_refs: The Muralla arabe de Madrid at the Cuesta de la Vega

stops.name: Cordoba, the patronymic written down in full
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the naming formula is standard across the Andalusi biographical dictionaries and belongs to no single dated act, so the placement here carries no source year
stops.campa: In the biographical dictionaries of al-Andalus the Cordoban astronomer is entered whole: Abu al-Qasim Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti. Sa'id al-Andalusi writes him so, and Ibn Bashkuwal, and Ibn al-Faradi, and Ibn Abi Usaybi'a after them. Ibn means son of. Ahmad is the father, a man of whom the record preserves nothing else whatever. Between one copyist and the next the middle of such a name can come loose, and a father with no biography can stand up out of his son's patronymic and walk off under his own name.
suggested_refs: Sa'id al-Andalusi, Tabaqat al-Umam; Ibn al-Faradi, Ta'rikh 'ulama' al-Andalus
sources: Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti', summarizing the Arabic biographical dictionaries

stops.name: Cordoba, the school of the exact sciences
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the school is attested, its founding year is not, and the address is unrecorded
stops.campa: Under the caliph al-Hakam II, Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti keeps a school of the exact sciences in Cordoba. He takes al-Khwarizmi's tables and converts them from Persian reckoning to the Hijri calendar; he works on the Arabic Almagest and on Ptolemy's Planisphaerium; he leaves behind methods of survey used on Andalusi ground. Ibn al-Saffar works in that room and dies at Denia in 1035. Sa'id al-Andalusi will call him the best mathematician and astronomer of his time in al-Andalus. Nobody who lists his books lists a book of talismans.
suggested_refs: The Cordoban school of exact sciences under al-Hakam II
sources: Sa'id al-Andalusi, Tabaqat al-Umam, as summarized in Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti'

stops.name: Basra, the epistles of an unnamed fraternity
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Rasa'il are placed in the mid-tenth century, and the Basra localization is doubted by part of the scholarship
stops.campa: A fraternity of scholars who withhold their names assembles fifty-one epistles on number, geometry, the stars, the soul, and the ranks of being, and signs the collection Ikhwan al-Safa, the Brethren of Purity. Tradition seats them in and around Basra; not everyone accepts the seating. The Rasa'il travel west without their authors, which is the habit of this whole corpus. Whoever writes the Rutbat al-Hakim in al-Andalus has read them closely enough to count them.
suggested_refs: Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa, the fifty-one epistles
sources: Wikipedia, 'Encyclopedia of the Brethren of Purity'

stops.name: Cordoba, the Rutbat al-Hakim closed in 343
stops.date_confidence: attested from the text's own preface, 343 AH, roughly 954 CE; Ritter argued the internal dates should be raised by about a century, to 443-448 AH
stops.campa: A book called Rutbat al-Hakim, the Rank of the Sage, is closed in al-Andalus in 343 of the Hijra. Its preface gives a course of study, a plan of work, and the count of the epistles it means to digest. It gives no name. The author speaks of what he has finished and of the companion volume he will begin next, and then the voice stops. Everything later said about the hand that held this pen is written onto the book from outside it, centuries after the ink dried.
stops.quote: Ya hemos presentado...51 epistolas en las que hemos reflexionado a fondo sobre esas ciencias
stops.quote_source: Rutbat al-Hakim, prologue, MS Besiraga 505, fol. 2b, in the Spanish translation of Godefroid de Callatay, Al-Qantara 34/2 (2013)
suggested_refs: MS Besiraga 505, the Rutbat al-Hakim prologue
sources: Godefroid de Callatay, 'Magia en al-Andalus', Al-Qantara 34/2 (2013)
David Pingree, Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes (1980)

stops.name: Cordoba, a summary of somebody else's encyclopedia
stops.date_confidence: attested from the same preface; the year is the text's own and is not corroborated outside it
stops.campa: The preface states plainly what kind of book this is: a digest of the many epistles that came before it. The claim is the hinge of the whole dispute. Whoever wrote the Rutba knew the Ikhwanian corpus intimately, and the men who reach al-Andalus carrying that corpus can be counted. De Callatay and Moureau will argue from this sentence, a thousand years on, that the writer is a Cordoban steeped in Batini letters rather than a caliphal astronomer correcting star tables.
stops.quote: Este libro nuestro...lo hemos concebido como un resumen de aquellas numerosas epistolas
stops.quote_source: Rutbat al-Hakim, prologue, MS Besiraga 505, fols. 3a-3b, in the Spanish translation of Godefroid de Callatay, Al-Qantara 34/2 (2013)
suggested_refs: The Rutba's self-description as a digest of the Rasa'il

stops.name: Cordoba, the vessel shaped like an egg
stops.date_confidence: undated within the text; the year follows the Rutba's own completion date and the experiment carries no date of its own
stops.campa: Inside the same anonymous book a man roasts mercury in a sealed glass and writes down what he sees: the quivering metal turns to a red powder, and the powder weighs what the metal weighed. Historians of chemistry read the sentence as an early statement that matter is conserved through change. The observation is exact, repeatable, and unsigned. It sits in a treatise on talismans, which is the reason the astronomers' guild will later be handed the credit for it.
stops.quote: I took natural quivering mercury, free from impurity, and placed it in a glass vessel shaped like an egg... The weight remaining as it was originally.
stops.quote_source: Rutbat al-Hakim, trans. E. J. Holmyard, Isis 6.3 (1924)
suggested_refs: The mercury calcination passage of the Rutbat al-Hakim

stops.name: Madinat al-Zahra, the palace-city in those decades
stops.date_confidence: attested for the site's occupation, built from 936 and active through al-Hakam II's reign of 961-976; no source places either book's author inside it
stops.campa: Four miles west of Cordoba the caliphs raise a city out of the hillside, with a library, a court, and a translation circle, and the Ghayat al-Hakim gives its own completion date squarely inside that court's working decades. No source puts the writer of either book within these walls. The palace is pillaged between 1010 and 1013 and left as terraces of cut stone. Whatever registers it held of who read what, and under whose patronage, go into the same fire.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Madinat al-Zahra, sacked between 1010 and 1013

stops.name: Cordoba, the Ghayat al-Hakim closed in 348
stops.date_confidence: attested from the Arabic text's own statement, 348 AH; Ritter proposed raising the internal dates by roughly a century, which would move composition to the 1050s and past the astronomer's death instead of before his adulthood
stops.campa: The companion volume announced in the Rutba's preface is finished five years later and calls itself Ghayat al-Hakim, the Aim of the Sage. It is a book of astral magic: images cut under particular skies, suffumigations, prayers to the planets, and long stretches copied out of the Brethren of Purity. It is also anonymous. Set the date against Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti's birth around 950 and the astronomer is nine years old when it closes. Set it against Ritter's raised chronology and the astronomer has been dead for decades.
suggested_refs: Ghayat al-Hakim, Arabic text, internal date 348 AH
sources: Hellmut Ritter (ed.), Studien der Bibliothek Warburg XII (1933)

stops.name: Cordoba, Maslama ibn Qasim al-Qurtubi is born
stops.date_confidence: attested in the biographical tradition as reported by Fierro; the year follows from a death in 964 at the age of fifty-eight and no month or day is given
stops.campa: A second Cordoban named Maslama is born forty-four years before the astronomer. He will keep no observatory and correct no tables. Ibn al-Faradi, who compiles the biographies of Andalusi scholars within living memory of him, files him under charms and talismans. Maribel Fierro will pull that single line out of the dictionary in 1996 and hang two books on it, and after her Paola Carusi, and after them De Callatay and Moureau with manuscripts in hand.
suggested_refs: Maslama ibn Qasim al-Qurtubi, born Cordoba 906

stops.name: Damascus, the Umayyad Mosque on the road east
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the sources place the start of al-Qurtubi's eastern travels before 932 and name Syria among the stages, without years for any single leg
stops.campa: Al-Qurtubi begins long travels before the year 932, and Syria is named among the stages. In the courtyard of the Umayyad Mosque the Andalusi scholar stands inside the mother city of the dynasty that his own Cordoba claims to continue, the same family, the same prayer, five thousand kilometres apart. Nothing survives of what he studied here or with whom. The itinerary comes from a few lines in a biographical dictionary, not from any travel diary he kept.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque of Damascus
sources: Fierro, Studia Islamica 84 (1996), as summarized in de.wikipedia.org, 'Picatrix'

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba on the pilgrim road
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Mecca is named among the stages of a journey begun before 932 and the year is placed within that window, not given by a source
stops.campa: Mecca stands in the list of his stages, as it stands in the list of every Andalusi scholar who turns east. He circles the House with the pilgrims of Khurasan and Ifriqiya and the Yemen, and the record of it is one word in a catalogue entry. Sixty years later the coordinates of this stone will be computed in Cordoba by Ibn al-Saffar so that the qibla can be set from Andalusi ground. One man walks to the stone; the other fixes it in numbers so that Cordoba can face it without leaving home.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Masjid al-Haram

stops.name: Baghdad, the Round City
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Baghdad is named among the stages of the pre-932 journey and the year is a placement within that window
stops.campa: Baghdad is named next, in the decades when the Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa are circulating out of the Iraqi schools and no copy has yet reached the far west. A man who walks through here in the 920s could carry that corpus home in his baggage, and the Ghayat al-Hakim quotes it at length. The connective tissue between this road and the writing of that book is inference, drawn taut by scholars who need it and admitted as inference by the honest ones among them. Nothing in the record puts a single volume in this traveller's hands.
suggested_refs: The Round City of al-Mansur, Karkh, Baghdad
sources: Fierro, Studia Islamica 84 (1996), as summarized in de.wikipedia.org, 'Picatrix'

stops.name: Sana'a, the Yemen and the loss of sight
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Yemen is the last named stage of a journey begun before 932 and closed by a return to Spain before his death in 964, with no year attached
stops.campa: Yemen closes the itinerary. In the Yemen, says the entry, this man loses his eyesight, and then he goes home. If the reattribution holds, the author of the most influential book of astral magic ever written in Arabic composes it blind, or dictates it, having seen the stars he writes about from four countries and then from none. No version of the Majriti tradition preserves this detail, because no version of the Majriti tradition is about him. The blindness survives in four words of a dictionary entry and nowhere else.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Sana'a
sources: Fierro, Studia Islamica 84 (1996), as summarized in Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti'

stops.name: Cordoba, the man of charms and talismans dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to 353 AH, 964 CE, in the biographical tradition reported by Fierro; no month or day is recorded and no grave is known
stops.campa: Maslama ibn Qasim al-Qurtubi dies in Cordoba in 353 of the Hijra, five years after the Ghayat al-Hakim says it was finished and ten after the Rutba. The arithmetic that breaks against the astronomer holds without strain for him. Ibn al-Faradi's dictionary, compiled within a generation, gives him four words that fit the two books exactly. The dictionary does not say he wrote them. That sentence has to be supplied by somebody, and nobody supplies it for a thousand years.
stops.quote: a man of charms and talismans
stops.quote_source: Ibn al-Faradi, Ta'rikh 'ulama' al-Andalus, on Maslama b. Qasim al-Qurtubi, as cited by Maribel Fierro, Studia Islamica 84 (1996), relayed through Wikipedia, 'Picatrix'
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Faradi's entry on Maslama b. Qasim al-Qurtubi

stops.name: Kairouan, the biographer takes the eastern road
stops.date_confidence: attested to the early 990s for Ibn al-Faradi's journey east; the individual stages carry no years
stops.campa: In the early 990s Ibn al-Faradi leaves al-Andalus and studies at Kairouan on his way east, sixty years after al-Qurtubi walked a comparable road and thirty before he himself will be killed in the sack of Cordoba. He is gathering the teachers, chains of transmission, and death dates that will become the first dictionary of Andalusi scholars. What he writes down is the closest thing to a contemporary record any figure in this dispute will ever get.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Uqba at Kairouan

stops.name: Cairo, the mosque of Amr at Fustat
stops.date_confidence: attested to the early 990s in the sequence Kairouan, Cairo, Mecca, Medina; no year is given for the Cairo stage
stops.campa: The road runs on through Fustat to Mecca and Medina, the standard circuit of an Andalusi scholar collecting hadith and authorizations. Four centuries later a Mamluk alchemist working a few streets from here will be the first man on record to write the name al-Majriti at the head of the Ghayat al-Hakim. Ibn al-Faradi, passing through with his notebooks four hundred years earlier, records no such thing about anybody. That silence, running from the men's own lifetimes to the alchemist's margin, is the strongest evidence the case has.
suggested_refs: The Mosque of Amr ibn al-As, Fustat

stops.name: Cordoba, the astronomer dies without the book
stops.date_confidence: contested: the sources give 395-398 AH, that is 1004 to 1008 CE, most often 1007 or 1008; the conflict is left open here
stops.campa: Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti dies in Cordoba somewhere between 1004 and 1008, and the dictionaries record the year without a grave. His works are counted at the time of death: the tables of al-Khwarizmi corrected, the Almagest improved, the Planisphaerium turned into Arabic, commercial arithmetic, a school full of students. Neither the Rutbat al-Hakim nor the Ghayat al-Hakim is on any of the lists, in any of the dictionaries, in the century that knew him.
suggested_refs: The lost tomb of Maslama al-Majriti at Cordoba

stops.name: Valencia, the dictionary of the scholars of al-Andalus
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Ibn al-Faradi serves as qadi of Valencia and compiles the Ta'rikh before his death in 1013, and the year here is a placement within that period
stops.campa: Ibn al-Faradi sits as qadi in Valencia and finishes the Ta'rikh ulama al-Andalus, some fifteen hundred lives of the scholars of the peninsula, before he is killed at Cordoba in 1013. The astronomer of Majrit is in it. The talisman-maker of Cordoba is in it. Neither is credited with the two books. Fierro will find in it, nine hundred years later, the four words about charms and talismans that reopen everything. Ibn al-Faradi could have asked men who knew them both. His book is the earliest place an attribution to a Majriti could stand, and it does not stand there.
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Faradi, Ta'rikh ulama al-Andalus

stops.name: Toledo, the verdict written sixty-one years late
stops.date_confidence: attested: Sa'id al-Andalusi completes the Tabaqat al-Umam in 1068, sixty-one years after the astronomer's death
stops.campa: In Toledo the qadi Sa'id al-Andalusi closes his survey of the nations and their sciences and gives the astronomer of Majrit the highest ranking in the book: best mathematician and astronomer of his time in al-Andalus. He knows the man's students, his corrections to the tables, his circle's work on the Brethren of Purity. He has no idea that three hundred years from now this same name will be printed on a manual of planetary talismans, and he leaves nothing in the entry that would let anyone put it there.
suggested_refs: Sa'id al-Andalusi, Tabaqat al-Umam, completed 1068
sources: Sa'id al-Andalusi, Tabaqat al-Umam, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti'

segments.name: The Name Fastened to the Book

stops.name: Tunis, the birth of the historian who will settle it
stops.date_confidence: attested: Ibn Khaldun is born at Tunis in 1332
stops.campa: Ibn Khaldun is born in Tunis into a family of Andalusi exiles from Seville. He will become the historian who explains how dynasties rise and rot. He tests chronicles against what is possible rather than against what is written, and lays down as a rule of the craft that any report must be measured against the nature of the thing reported. On the question of who wrote the Ghayat al-Hakim he will apply none of this, and his sentence will stand for six hundred years.
suggested_refs: Ibn Khaldun's birthplace in the Tunis medina

stops.name: Cairo, an alchemist writes a name on the book
stops.date_confidence: contested: al-Jildaki's death is given as 743 AH, that is 1342, by Brockelmann and as shortly after 1360 by the manuscript literature; the earlier date is not reconciled here
stops.campa: Aydamur al-Jildaki, a Mamluk alchemist at work in Cairo, produces the earliest known manuscript attribution of the Ghayat al-Hakim to a scholar called al-Majriti. Four centuries stand between the book's own stated date and this line. He does not say which al-Majriti, gives no chain of transmission, and cites nothing earlier. No surviving source before him makes the claim at all. From here it is simply repeated, and repetition is what the tradition takes for evidence.
suggested_refs: Al-Jildaki's alchemical corpus, earliest carrier of the al-Majriti attribution

stops.name: Qal'at Ibn Salama, the Muqaddimah drafted in a fortress
stops.date_confidence: attested for the composition of the Muqaddimah in 1377, written during a retreat of over three years, from 1375 to 1378; the fortress site is a traditional identification and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: Shut up in a fortress in western Algeria for three years, out of reach of the courts he has served and betrayed, Ibn Khaldun writes the prolegomena to his universal history. In the chapters on magic and the occult sciences he names the man who summarized the whole art in one book and calls him Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti, imam of the Andalusis in mathematics and in magic. The patronymic is right there in the sentence that makes the mistake. Nobody checks the arithmetic for five hundred years.
stops.quote: Luego vino Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti, el imam de los andalusies por las matematicas y por la magia. Hizo el resumen de todas esas obras...llamado 'El Objetivo del sabio'
stops.quote_source: Ibn Khaldun, Kitab al-'ibar, I, p. 497, in the Spanish translation of Godefroid de Callatay, Al-Qantara 34/2 (2013)
suggested_refs: Qal'at Ibn Salama, near Frenda, where the Muqaddimah was drafted
sources: Ibn Khaldun, Kitab al-'ibar, as translated in de Callatay, Al-Qantara 34/2 (2013)

stops.name: Cairo, al-Azhar and the revisions of an old man
stops.date_confidence: attested: Ibn Khaldun reaches Cairo in Sha'ban 782 AH, that is 1380, and dies there in 1406; the report that he taught at al-Azhar comes secondhand through al-Sakhawi
stops.campa: Ibn Khaldun settles in Cairo for the last twenty-six years of his life, teaches, sits as Maliki qadi six separate times, and keeps revising the history. The attribution stays in. Through the Cairo manuscript trade it reaches every later Arabic writer who touches the subject, and through them the European orientalists who will one day sit down to sort the Majriti names apart. The error is not hidden anywhere. It is in the most widely copied Arabic prose work of the age.
suggested_refs: Al-Azhar Mosque, Cairo, and Ibn Khaldun's Egyptian career

stops.name: Toledo, Alfonso X orders the Ghaya into Castilian
stops.date_confidence: attested only as a window: the Latin prologue says the translation was made by order of Alfonso X at some time between 1256 and 1258, and no source dates a commission or a completion within it
stops.campa: Alfonso X of Castile, who is having the stars, the stones, and the games of the world put into Castilian, orders the Ghayat al-Hakim translated among a small group of magical works. Yehuda ben Moshe does the work, alongside the Lapidario and the Libro de las formas et las ymagenes. Of that group only the Lapidario survives entire. The Castilian Ghaya is lost, and everything Latin Europe will know of the book descends from a text nobody has seen since.
suggested_refs: The Alfonsine translation workshop and the lost Castilian Ghaya

stops.name: Seville, the court that will not sit still
stops.date_confidence: not established: no source consulted names the city where the Castilian translation was made, and the Alfonsine court was itinerant between Toledo, Seville, and Burgos
stops.campa: The king's court moves with the king. Seville is his favourite city and his burial place, and the workshops of translators follow the household rather than any fixed address. Which room the Ghaya was turned into Castilian in, and whether the translator worked from one Arabic manuscript or several, the record does not say. A book about the exact hour and the exact image is handed on without an exact place, an exact date, or an exact author. Only the window survives, three years wide, taken from a prologue written by somebody else in another language.
suggested_refs: The itinerant court of Alfonso X

stops.name: Toledo, the Latin book gets a name nobody can explain
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Latin version is made from the Castilian shortly after 1258 and neither the translator nor the year is recorded
stops.campa: Out of the lost Castilian a Latin version is made, in the translation culture that has been moving Arabic science north from Toledo for over a century. The translator leaves no name. The book acquires a title, Picatrix, that nobody has ever satisfactorily explained. It enters Latin Europe under a garbled title and no translator's name, its Castilian intermediary already lost. The author printed on it is a Cordoban astronomer who was a child when the Arabic says the book was written.
suggested_refs: The Latin Picatrix and its unnamed translator

stops.name: Krakow, a copy among the northern manuscripts
stops.date_confidence: not established: the Jagiellonian holding is asserted from the general manuscript tradition rather than from confirmed shelf-mark research, and the century is a placement
stops.campa: The Latin Picatrix spreads by copy across Catholic Europe, into libraries at Krakow, Munich, Paris, and Rome, read by astrologers, physicians, and the occasional nervous theologian. Each copy carries the author's name forward without question. The manuscript diffusion is wide and its individual holdings are poorly catalogued; several of the shelf marks repeated in the modern literature go unverified when anyone tries to check them, including this one.
suggested_refs: The Jagiellonian Library, Krakow
sources: Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', for the general manuscript tradition; the specific holding is unverified

stops.name: Florence, Careggi and the astral physicians
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication of De Vita Coelitus Comparanda in 1489; the extent of its direct debt to the Picatrix is debated among historians of Renaissance magic
stops.campa: At the Medici villa above Florence, Marsilio Ficino publishes a book on drawing life down from the heavens: talismanic images, planetary music, the right hour for the right remedy. It is the same art the Ghayat al-Hakim set out in Arabic five centuries before, arriving through channels Ficino does not fully name. How much he took from the Picatrix directly and how much from the wider current the Picatrix fed is argued over and unsettled. The name on the Arabic book means nothing to him.
suggested_refs: Marsilio Ficino, De Vita Coelitus Comparanda (1489)
sources: General history of Renaissance astral magic; the direct textual debt is not verified against a primary Ficino citation here

stops.name: London, the book among the English astrologers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the chain of ownership across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; the pin stands for England rather than a fixed address
stops.campa: A Picatrix manuscript passes from hand to hand through the English occultists: Simon Forman, then Richard Napier, then Elias Ashmole, then William Lilly, each casting figures, each copying passages, each believing he holds the work of a Spanish Moor named Maslama. Not one of them has any means of checking. The Arabic original is unavailable in Europe, and will stay unavailable until an orientalist stumbles on a complete manuscript three hundred years later.
suggested_refs: The Ashmole and Lilly manuscripts of the Latin Picatrix

segments.name: The Philologists Take the Name Apart

stops.name: Halle, the catalogue of everything written in Arabic
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Brockelmann's Geschichte der Arabischen Litteratur appears in editions and supplements between 1898 and 1949, and no single year applies
stops.campa: Carl Brockelmann builds the bibliographic catalogue of Arabic letters, author by author, manuscript by manuscript, in a form that lets a scholar in Berlin or Leiden see at a glance what is attributed to whom and where the copies sit. It is against entries like these, rather than against any documented biography of a man called Ahmad al-Majriti, that the next four generations argue. The catalogue can record a name. It cannot tell whether the name ever belonged to anybody.
suggested_refs: Carl Brockelmann, Geschichte der Arabischen Litteratur
sources: Standard reference status of Brockelmann's GAL; the specific entry content is not verified here

stops.name: Berlin, an Arabic manuscript surfaces
stops.date_confidence: attested to in or around 1920 for Printz's discovery; neither the exact year nor the library is named in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Wilhelm Printz finds a complete Arabic text of the Ghayat al-Hakim and makes it known in German orientalist circles. Until this moment Europe has argued about the Picatrix for six hundred years without access to the original. The Latin can now be laid beside the Arabic, and the Arabic carries a preface with dates in it. Every reattribution and every retraction after him comes out of that recovered preface and its two Hijri years. Printz does not name the library he found it in, or else the sources reporting him drop the name, and the recovery itself stays half documented.
suggested_refs: Wilhelm Printz's rediscovery of the Arabic Ghayat al-Hakim, c. 1920

stops.name: Istanbul, the manuscripts and the man who catalogued them
stops.date_confidence: not established: no source consulted names an Istanbul library for the manuscript behind Ritter's edition, though Ritter lived and catalogued collections in the city from 1926 to 1949 and the Rutba manuscript later cited by De Callatay, Besiraga 505, belongs to an Istanbul collection
stops.campa: Hellmut Ritter moves to Istanbul and spends twenty-three years in its manuscript collections, cataloguing what the Ottoman libraries hold. The Rutbat al-Hakim copy that will supply the crucial prologue quotations, Besiraga 505, sits in this city. Whether the Ghaya manuscript that Ritter edits also comes from here is not stated by any source consulted, only made plausible by where he was standing for twenty-three years. The Suleymaniye is often given as the library that held it, and nothing in the record supports that either.
suggested_refs: MS Besiraga 505, Istanbul; Ritter's Ottoman manuscript catalogues
sources: de Callatay, Al-Qantara 34/2 (2013), for MS Besiraga 505; the provenance of Ritter's Ghaya manuscript is unverified

stops.name: Hamburg, the library on the Heilwigstrasse
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1933 Arabic edition, Studien der Bibliothek Warburg XII; the imprint is Teubner, Leipzig and Berlin, and Hamburg is the seat of the series' parent library rather than the place of printing
stops.campa: The critical Arabic text of the Ghayat al-Hakim is edited by Ritter and printed in the series of a private Hamburg library built to study how the images and the astrology of the ancient world survived into Europe. The book it publishes is the missing Arabic hinge of exactly that question. Ritter argues that the internal dates cannot stand as written and proposes raising them by about a century. Either way, the man from Majrit did not write it. That same year the library is packed into two steamers and leaves Germany.
suggested_refs: Hellmut Ritter (ed.), Ghayat al-Hakim, Studien der Bibliothek Warburg XII (1933)
sources: Bibliographic record, Teubner, Leipzig and Berlin, 1933

stops.name: London, the author is given a name meaning no name
stops.date_confidence: attested: Ritter and Martin Plessner, Picatrix: Das Ziel des Weisen von Pseudo-Magriti, Studies of the Warburg Institute 27, London 1962
stops.campa: Twenty-nine years after the library's flight, now an institute of the University of London, Ritter and Martin Plessner publish the German translation. The title page settles the authorship question in the only honest way available: von Pseudo-Magriti, by the false Majriti. A term of art is minted for a hole in the record. From here on the scholarship has a way to name the author without claiming to know him, and the popular literature goes on printing Ahmad and Maslama as if the hole had never been noticed.
suggested_refs: Ritter and Plessner, Picatrix: Das Ziel des Weisen von Pseudo-Magriti (1962)
sources: Bibliographic record, Studies of the Warburg Institute 27, London 1962

stops.name: Providence, the Latin text collated at last
stops.date_confidence: attested: Pingree, Picatrix: The Latin Version of the Ghayat al-Hakim, Studies of the Warburg Institute 39, London 1986; his source-study article appeared in the Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes in 1980
stops.campa: David Pingree, at Brown University, traces the Hermetic, Sabian, and Greek astrological material inside the Ghaya and then edits the Latin version out of its scattered manuscripts, the first critical text the Picatrix has had in seven centuries of copying. He rejects the al-Majriti attribution on the internal evidence and says so. The book that Europe read as the work of a named Andalusi sage is now readable, for the first time, as the work of nobody in particular.
suggested_refs: Pingree, Picatrix: The Latin Version of the Ghayat al-Hakim (1986)
sources: David Pingree, Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes (1980)

stops.name: Madrid, a candidate is named out of a dictionary entry
stops.date_confidence: attested: Fierro, Studia Islamica 84 (1996), pp. 87-112; the pin marks the CSIC campus on Calle Serrano, and her institute in 1996 was the Instituto de Filologia
stops.campa: Maribel Fierro, at the Spanish research council, publishes the article that turns a negative finding into a positive one. Her candidate is the other Cordoban Maslama, dead in 964, whom Ibn al-Faradi files under charms and talismans, and whose Batini and Sufi milieu fits the two books where the astronomer's observatory never did. The dates work, the description works, the city works. She proposes it. She does not claim to have closed it, and it is not closed.
suggested_refs: Fierro, 'Batinism in al-Andalus', Studia Islamica 84 (1996), pp. 87-112

stops.name: Rome, alchemy argued back into its religion
stops.date_confidence: attested for Paola Carusi, 'Alchimia islamica e religione', Oriente Moderno 19/3 (2000), pp. 461-502; the German literature cites her alongside Fierro for the alternative authorship
stops.campa: Paola Carusi, working in Rome on how Islamic alchemy argued for its own legitimacy as a science of nature, is cited alongside Fierro in support of the alternative author. Her form of the candidate's name keeps the nisba attached: Maslama ibn al-Qasim al-Majriti. The reattribution does not evict the word al-Majriti from the case; it detaches the word from the astronomer and leaves two men of one city wearing the same adjective. The nisba was never the problem. The given name was, and that is the part the copyists handled worst.
suggested_refs: Paola Carusi, Oriente Moderno 19/3 (2000), pp. 461-502

stops.name: Madrid, two manuscripts of the Rutba go to press
stops.date_confidence: attested: De Callatay and Moureau, Al-Qantara 37/2 (2016); the pin marks the CSIC, which publishes Al-Qantara, and not the authors' own university
stops.campa: Godefroid de Callatay and Sebastien Moureau bring two manuscripts of the Rutbat al-Hakim into the argument and report what the Andalusi habit actually was: to credit the astronomer not only with the two magical books but with the whole encyclopedia of the Brethren of Purity as well. One famous name absorbing the unsigned work of a whole century. Five years later De Callatay is still testing it, sentence against sentence, and still finding the question open at the edges.
stops.quote: As a continuation of previous studies about the reception of Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa' in al-Andalus, this paper argues that it was common among Andalusi scholars of the Middle Ages to credit the astronomer Maslama al-Majriti (d. 395/1004 or shortly thereafter) not only with the authorship of Rutbat al-Hakim and Ghayat al-Hakim - now both correctly ascribed to Maslama Ibn Qasim al-Qurtubi (d. 353/964) - but also with the entire encyclopaedic corpus of the Rasa'il.
stops.quote_source: De Callatay and Moureau, 'De nuevo sobre Maslama Ibn Qasim al-Qurtubi, los Ijwan al-Safa' e Ibn Jaldun', Al-Qantara 37/2 (2016), abstract
suggested_refs: De Callatay and Moureau, Al-Qantara 37/2 (2016); de Callatay, Arabica 68/5-6 (2021)

stops.name: Cordoba, the search that returns nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested as a negative finding of searches conducted in August 2026; absence of an entry is not proof that no such person existed
stops.campa: Ask the reference works for Ahmad al-Majriti and nothing comes back. No entry, no dates, no city, no works. The bare nisba redirects to the astronomer, whose father was called Ahmad and about whom the record is otherwise silent. The likeliest account is the plainest: a patronymic came loose in the copying, was read as a given name, and was catalogued as a person. Whether that is a scribal ghost or a genuinely separate man, no source consulted can say, and none pretends to.
suggested_refs: The absent entry: no standalone notice for Ahmad al-Majriti in any reference work consulted
sources: Searches of en.wikipedia.org and britannica.com, August 2026, returning no distinct entry

stops.name: Madrid, the nisba still in circulation
stops.date_confidence: attested as an observed pattern across encyclopedic, semi-scholarly, and esoteric-tradition sources consulted in 2026
stops.campa: A century of philology has produced three names for one book, and the popular literature uses all three interchangeably: Ahmad al-Majriti, Maslama al-Majriti, and the empty courtesy Pseudo-Majriti. Editions of the Picatrix go on appearing in English and French with a Cordoban author on the title page. The town on the Manzanares is now a capital of five million people, and the adjective made from its old Arabic name still travels, still attached to a book, still attached to no one at all.
suggested_refs: Modern editions of the Picatrix and their title-page attributions
